CC1.1.o: Every other control rests on people behaving honestly. Leadership sets that tone, and it has to be written down and enforced, not assumed.
CC1.1.a: Publish a code of conduct, have every employee and contractor acknowledge it at hiring and every year, and deal with breaches of it consistently.
CC1.1.e: They inspect the code of conduct, sample new hires and current staff for signed acknowledgements, and ask how violations were handled.
CC1.1.r: Code of conduct; acknowledgement records; disciplinary policy; any investigations log.

CC1.2.o: Someone above day-to-day management has to watch whether controls work. In a small company this can be the board, an advisory board or the owners.
CC1.2.a: Name the governing body, set out its oversight duties in a charter, and have it meet at least quarterly with security and risk on the agenda.
CC1.2.e: They read the charter and minutes for the period and look for evidence that security, risk and audit results were discussed.
CC1.2.r: Board or committee charter; meeting minutes; security reports presented to the board.

CC1.3.o: People need to know who is responsible for what, who they report to, and who can approve what.
CC1.3.a: Keep a current organisation chart, write job descriptions with security responsibilities, and name owners for security, privacy and compliance.
CC1.3.e: They inspect the organisation chart and job descriptions and check that key roles were filled during the period.
CC1.3.r: Organisation chart; job descriptions; RACI or role assignments; appointment letters for security roles.

CC1.4.o: Controls only work if the people running them know how. That means hiring checks, training and performance reviews.
CC1.4.a: Run background checks before hiring, give security awareness training at onboarding and every year, and hold yearly performance reviews.
CC1.4.e: They sample new hires for background checks and training completion, and current staff for annual training and reviews.
CC1.4.r: Background check records; training completion reports; performance review records; hiring procedure.

CC1.5.o: Responsibilities on paper mean little unless people are measured against them and consequences follow.
CC1.5.a: Include control duties in job descriptions and reviews, and apply the disciplinary policy when someone ignores them.
CC1.5.e: They look for performance criteria that include control duties and for evidence that the disciplinary process was used where needed.
CC1.5.r: Performance review templates; disciplinary policy; sanctions records.

CC2.1.o: Controls depend on information that is accurate, complete and on time: logs, reports, inventories and tickets.
CC2.1.a: Identify the information each key control needs, where it comes from, and how you know it is complete and accurate. Keep system inventories and data flow diagrams current.
CC2.1.e: They test the completeness and accuracy of reports used in controls, and inspect inventories and data flow diagrams.
CC2.1.r: System inventory; data flow diagrams; report validation notes; log retention settings.

CC2.2.o: Staff cannot follow policies they have never seen or report problems if they do not know how.
CC2.2.a: Publish policies where staff can find them, communicate security responsibilities at onboarding and yearly, and give people a way to report incidents and concerns, including anonymously.
CC2.2.e: They inspect the policy portal, onboarding material and communications, and confirm a reporting channel exists and is known.
CC2.2.r: Intranet or policy portal; policy acknowledgements; security newsletters; whistleblowing or reporting procedure.

CC2.3.o: Customers need to know your commitments, how to report problems and how changes affect them. Vendors need to know your requirements.
CC2.3.a: Publish a system description, terms of service and security commitments, give customers a channel to report incidents, and tell them about changes that affect them.
CC2.3.e: They inspect contracts, terms, the public security page, customer notifications and the external reporting channel.
CC2.3.r: Customer contracts and terms; security or trust page; customer notification records; support contact details.

CC3.1.o: A risk is only a risk to something. The company needs stated objectives, including its service commitments and system requirements.
CC3.1.a: Write down your service commitments to customers and the system requirements that meet them, and review them each year.
CC3.1.e: They read the documented objectives and service commitments and check they are consistent with contracts and the system description.
CC3.1.r: Service commitments and system requirements; strategy or objectives document; annual review record.

CC3.2.o: You need a regular, documented look at what could go wrong, how likely it is and how bad it would be.
CC3.2.a: Run a formal risk assessment at least once a year covering technology, people, vendors and processes. Score each risk and decide how to treat it.
CC3.2.e: They inspect the risk assessment for the period, its methodology, and evidence that treatment decisions were made and followed up.
CC3.2.r: Risk assessment methodology; risk register; treatment plans; approval by management.

CC3.3.o: Fraud includes theft of assets, false reporting and management overriding controls. It needs its own look.
CC3.3.a: Include fraud scenarios in the risk assessment: misuse of privileged access, manipulated reports, insider theft and collusion.
CC3.3.e: They check that the risk assessment explicitly considers fraud and that related risks have controls.
CC3.3.r: Fraud risk section of the risk assessment; related controls.

CC3.4.o: New products, acquisitions, new technology, leadership changes and regulation can all make existing controls inadequate.
CC3.4.a: Review significant changes as they happen and in the annual risk assessment, and update controls when needed.
CC3.4.e: They look for evidence that significant changes during the period were assessed for risk.
CC3.4.r: Change risk assessments; risk register updates; meeting minutes discussing significant change.

CC4.1.o: Controls drift. Ongoing monitoring and periodic separate evaluations catch that before the auditor does.
CC4.1.a: Run internal control reviews or internal audits, automated compliance monitoring, and periodic penetration tests and vulnerability scans.
CC4.1.e: They inspect internal audit reports, monitoring dashboards and penetration test reports from the period.
CC4.1.r: Internal audit reports; control self-assessments; penetration test and scan reports.

CC4.2.o: Finding a weakness is only useful if the right people hear about it and it is fixed.
CC4.2.a: Log every deficiency found, give it an owner and a due date, report open items to management, and track them to closure.
CC4.2.e: They sample deficiencies from the period and check they were communicated, assigned and remediated on time.
CC4.2.r: Findings register; remediation tickets; management reports on open findings.

CC5.1.o: Each significant risk should be matched by controls that actually reduce it, with a mix of preventive and detective controls.
CC5.1.a: Map risks to controls, check every significant risk is covered, and consider segregation of duties.
CC5.1.e: They inspect the risk-to-control mapping and look for significant risks without controls.
CC5.1.r: Risk and control matrix; segregation of duties analysis.

CC5.2.o: Technology runs most controls, so the technology itself needs controls over access, change and operations.
CC5.2.a: Define IT general controls for access, change management, operations and infrastructure security, and link each to the systems in scope.
CC5.2.e: They inspect the IT general controls and confirm they cover all in-scope systems.
CC5.2.r: IT general controls list; system inventory with in-scope flag.

CC5.3.o: A control exists when a policy says what should happen and a procedure says how, and people follow it.
CC5.3.a: Keep an approved set of security policies, review them every year, assign an owner to each, and back them with procedures.
CC5.3.e: They inspect the policies for approval and review dates, and test that procedures are followed.
CC5.3.r: Policy set with version history; approval records; procedures and runbooks.

CC6.1.o: Systems holding customer data need authentication, network controls and encryption so only the right people and systems get in.
CC6.1.a: Keep an inventory of in-scope systems, enforce single sign-on and multi-factor authentication, use strong password settings, segment networks and encrypt data at rest.
CC6.1.e: They inspect authentication settings, MFA enforcement, encryption configuration and network design for in-scope systems.
CC6.1.r: Asset inventory; SSO and MFA configuration; password policy settings; encryption at rest settings; network diagrams.

CC6.2.o: Accounts should only exist for people whose access was approved, and should be removed when they leave.
CC6.2.a: Require a documented, approved request for every new account, and remove access within a set time (for example one business day) when someone leaves.
CC6.2.e: They sample new joiners for approved access requests and leavers for timely removal across in-scope systems.
CC6.2.r: Access request tickets; HR joiner and leaver lists; deprovisioning tickets; system account lists.

CC6.3.o: People should have only the access their job needs, and that access should change when their job does.
CC6.3.a: Define roles, grant access by role, restrict admin rights, and review all user access at least every quarter.
CC6.3.e: They inspect the role definitions, sample access changes, and inspect quarterly access reviews and the actions taken from them.
CC6.3.r: Role matrix; access review records with sign-off; tickets for access removed after review.

CC6.4.o: Physical access to offices, server rooms and data centres must be limited to authorised people.
CC6.4.a: Use badges or locks, keep visitor logs, review physical access lists, and for cloud hosting rely on the provider's SOC report.
CC6.4.e: They inspect badge access lists and reviews, visitor logs, and the cloud provider's SOC 2 report.
CC6.4.r: Badge access lists; physical access reviews; visitor logs; data centre provider SOC report.

CC6.5.o: Old laptops, disks and backups can leak data long after they leave use.
CC6.5.a: Wipe or destroy media before disposal or reuse, use certified disposal vendors, and keep certificates of destruction.
CC6.5.e: They sample disposed assets and inspect wiping or destruction certificates.
CC6.5.r: Asset disposal log; certificates of destruction; media sanitisation procedure.

CC6.6.o: Internet-facing systems face constant attack and need firewalls, secure remote access and intrusion protection.
CC6.6.a: Use firewalls or security groups with default deny, require VPN or zero-trust access for admin, use a web application firewall, and review rules regularly.
CC6.6.e: They inspect firewall rules, remote access configuration and periodic rule reviews.
CC6.6.r: Firewall and security group rules; rule review records; VPN or ZTNA configuration; WAF settings.

CC6.7.o: Data in transit and data leaving the company on devices or media must be protected.
CC6.7.a: Enforce TLS for data in transit, encrypt laptops and mobile devices, restrict removable media, and use data loss prevention where it fits.
CC6.7.e: They inspect TLS configuration, device encryption reports and removable media settings.
CC6.7.r: TLS configuration and scan results; MDM encryption reports; DLP or USB policy settings.

CC6.8.o: Malware and unapproved software are a common way in.
CC6.8.a: Run endpoint protection on every device and server, keep it updated, restrict software installation, and alert on detections.
CC6.8.e: They inspect endpoint protection coverage and settings, and sample alerts to check they were handled.
CC6.8.r: EDR or antivirus coverage report; software installation policy; malware alert tickets.

CC7.1.o: Unknown changes and unpatched vulnerabilities are how most systems are compromised.
CC7.1.a: Scan for vulnerabilities at least monthly, track configuration against a baseline, and patch within set timelines by severity.
CC7.1.e: They inspect scan results, configuration monitoring and evidence that critical findings were fixed on time.
CC7.1.r: Vulnerability scan reports; patching SLAs; remediation tickets; configuration baseline and drift alerts.

CC7.2.o: You need to notice attacks and failures while they happen.
CC7.2.a: Collect logs centrally, define alerts for suspicious activity, and have someone review and respond to alerts.
CC7.2.e: They inspect logging configuration, alert rules and samples of alerts with their follow-up.
CC7.2.r: SIEM or log platform configuration; alert rules; alert tickets; on-call schedule.

CC7.3.o: Not every alert is an incident. A consistent triage process decides which are and how serious.
CC7.3.a: Write an incident response plan with severity levels and triage criteria, and record the decision on each event.
CC7.3.e: They inspect the incident response plan and sample events to check triage was done and recorded.
CC7.3.r: Incident response plan; triage records; incident register.

CC7.4.o: When an incident is confirmed, people need to know who leads, how to contain it, and who to tell.
CC7.4.a: Follow the incident response plan: contain, eradicate, communicate to customers where required, and run a post-incident review. Test the plan every year.
CC7.4.e: They sample incidents to check the plan was followed, and inspect the annual tabletop exercise.
CC7.4.r: Incident tickets and timelines; customer notifications; post-incident reviews; tabletop exercise report.

CC7.5.o: After an incident the system must be restored and the cause fixed so it does not happen again.
CC7.5.a: Restore affected systems, confirm integrity, record lessons learned, and turn them into control or process changes.
CC7.5.e: They inspect post-incident reviews and confirm that corrective actions were tracked to closure.
CC7.5.r: Post-incident reviews; corrective action tickets; restoration records.

CC8.1.o: Uncontrolled changes are a leading cause of outages and security gaps. Every change to production should be planned and approved.
CC8.1.a: Use version control and a ticket for every change, require peer review and testing, separate development from production, restrict who can deploy, and handle emergency changes with after-the-fact approval.
CC8.1.e: They sample production changes for ticket, review, testing and approval, and check that developers cannot push unreviewed code to production.
CC8.1.r: Change management policy; pull requests with approvals; CI/CD pipeline settings; branch protection; emergency change log.

CC9.1.o: Outages, disasters and key-person loss need plans that keep commitments to customers.
CC9.1.a: Write a business continuity and disaster recovery plan, consider cyber insurance, and test the plans every year.
CC9.1.e: They inspect the BC/DR plans, test results and insurance where it is part of the risk response.
CC9.1.r: Business continuity plan; disaster recovery plan; test reports; insurance policy summary.

CC9.2.o: Vendors that touch your data or systems carry your risk. Some of them are subservice organisations named in your report.
CC9.2.a: Keep a vendor inventory, assess vendors before onboarding and each year by risk, get their SOC reports or equivalent, and put security terms in contracts.
CC9.2.e: They inspect the vendor inventory, sample vendor reviews and SOC report reviews, and check contracts for security terms.
CC9.2.r: Vendor inventory with risk ratings; vendor assessments; reviewed vendor SOC reports with complementary controls noted; contracts.

A1.1.o: If demand outgrows capacity, the system slows down or fails.
A1.1.a: Monitor processing capacity and usage, set thresholds and alerts, use autoscaling where possible, and plan capacity ahead.
A1.1.e: They inspect capacity monitoring, thresholds and alerts, and evidence of capacity planning.
A1.1.r: Monitoring dashboards; alert thresholds; autoscaling configuration; capacity plans.

A1.2.o: Availability depends on resilient infrastructure, environmental protections and reliable backups.
A1.2.a: Run regular backups with monitoring for failures, replicate across zones or regions, and rely on the hosting provider's environmental protections.
A1.2.e: They inspect backup configuration and job monitoring, redundancy design, and the provider's SOC report.
A1.2.r: Backup configuration and logs; failure alerts; multi-zone architecture; hosting provider SOC report.

A1.3.o: A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a control.
A1.3.a: Test restoring from backup and run the disaster recovery plan at least once a year, record the results and fix what failed.
A1.3.e: They inspect restore tests and DR test reports from the period.
A1.3.r: Restore test records; DR test report with recovery times achieved; follow-up actions.

C1.1.o: You can only protect confidential information if you know what it is and where it lives.
C1.1.a: Classify data, label or inventory confidential information, restrict access to it, and encrypt it.
C1.1.e: They inspect the data classification policy and the inventory of confidential data with its protections.
C1.1.r: Data classification policy; confidential data inventory; access restrictions; NDAs.

C1.2.o: Keeping confidential data past its use adds risk with no benefit.
C1.2.a: Set retention periods, delete or destroy confidential data at the end of them or on customer request, and record that you did.
C1.2.e: They inspect the retention schedule and sample deletion requests and disposals.
C1.2.r: Retention schedule; deletion logs; customer deletion confirmations; certificates of destruction.

PI1.1.o: Processing integrity needs a definition of what complete, accurate and timely means for your service.
PI1.1.a: Document processing specifications, data definitions and service levels, and share what customers need to know.
PI1.1.e: They inspect the processing specifications and customer-facing documentation.
PI1.1.r: Processing specifications; data dictionary; product documentation; SLAs.

PI1.2.o: Errors that enter at input travel all the way to output.
PI1.2.a: Validate inputs with edit checks, reject or flag bad records, and track rejections to resolution.
PI1.2.e: They inspect input validation rules and sample rejected or flagged inputs.
PI1.2.r: Input validation rules; error logs; rejection reports.

PI1.3.o: Processing must do what the specification says, every time.
PI1.3.a: Use automated checks such as record counts and control totals, monitor jobs, and investigate failures.
PI1.3.e: They inspect job monitoring, reconciliation of control totals and failed job handling.
PI1.3.r: Batch job monitoring; reconciliation reports; incident tickets for failed processing.

PI1.4.o: Output that is wrong, late or sent to the wrong recipient breaks commitments.
PI1.4.a: Reconcile outputs to inputs, review outputs before release where needed, and restrict who receives them.
PI1.4.e: They inspect output reconciliations and distribution controls.
PI1.4.r: Output reconciliations; distribution lists; delivery logs.

PI1.5.o: Data at rest during processing must not be lost or altered.
PI1.5.a: Protect stored data with access controls and integrity checks, and keep it for the agreed period.
PI1.5.e: They inspect storage controls, integrity checks and retention settings.
PI1.5.r: Storage configuration; integrity checks such as checksums; retention settings.

P1.1.o: People have a right to know what personal information you collect, why, and what choices they have.
P1.1.a: Publish a clear privacy notice, keep it current, and make it available where data is collected.
P1.1.e: They inspect the privacy notice, its version history and where it is shown.
P1.1.r: Privacy notice with versions; screenshots of where it is presented.

P2.1.o: Where processing depends on consent, people must be able to give it and take it back.
P2.1.a: Record consent where required, make withdrawal easy, and respect withdrawal in your systems.
P2.1.e: They inspect consent mechanisms and sample consent and withdrawal records.
P2.1.r: Consent records; preference centre configuration; withdrawal handling.

P3.1.o: Collecting less means less to protect.
P3.1.a: Limit collection to what the stated purposes need, and review forms and data feeds for extra fields.
P3.1.e: They compare what is collected against the stated purposes.

P3.2.o: Some information, such as health data, needs explicit consent before you collect it.
P3.2.a: Identify sensitive information you collect and get and record explicit consent for it.
P3.2.e: They inspect consent records for sensitive information.
P3.2.r: Sensitive data inventory; explicit consent records.

P4.1.o: Data collected for one reason should not quietly be used for another.
P4.1.a: Tie each use of personal information to a stated purpose, and assess any new use before starting.
P4.1.e: They inspect data use against the privacy notice and review new-use assessments.

P4.2.o: Retention limits reduce the damage of any breach.
P4.2.a: Set a retention period for each category of personal information and enforce it.
P4.2.e: They inspect the retention schedule and evidence it is applied.
P4.2.r: Retention schedule; automated deletion jobs; deletion logs.

P4.3.o: Personal information must be unrecoverable once disposed of.
P4.3.a: Use secure deletion and destruction methods and record disposals.
P4.3.e: They inspect disposal procedures and sample disposal records.
P4.3.r: Disposal procedure; deletion logs; certificates of destruction.

P5.1.o: People can ask what you hold about them.
P5.1.a: Have a process to verify identity and answer access requests within the time promised.
P5.1.e: They sample access requests for identity checks and on-time answers.
P5.1.r: Request log; responses; identity verification records.

P5.2.o: Wrong information can harm people and must be fixed when they ask.
P5.2.a: Have a process to correct information on request and tell anyone it was shared with where needed.
P5.2.e: They sample correction requests and how they were handled.

P6.1.o: Disclosing data to others must match what people were told and agreed to.
P6.1.a: List the third parties you share with, why, and on what basis, and check new disclosures against the notice.
P6.1.e: They inspect the list of third-party disclosures against the privacy notice.
P6.1.r: Third-party sharing inventory; data processing agreements.

P6.2.o: You must be able to show what you disclosed, to whom and when.
P6.2.a: Keep a log of disclosures to third parties, including those required by law.

P6.3.o: Every breach or unauthorised disclosure must be recorded, even small ones.
P6.3.a: Keep a breach and unauthorised disclosure log with what happened, impact and actions.
P6.3.e: They inspect the log and compare it with incident records.

P6.4.o: Vendors who process personal information for you must protect it to your standard.
P6.4.a: Put privacy and security obligations into contracts with vendors handling personal information and review them.
P6.4.e: They sample vendor contracts for privacy terms.

P6.5.o: You can only notify people if your vendors tell you about their incidents.
P6.5.a: Require vendors in contract to notify you of breaches within a set time.
P6.5.e: They inspect contract terms for breach notification.

P6.6.o: When a breach affects people, they and sometimes regulators must be told on time.
P6.6.a: Include breach notification steps and timelines in the incident response plan and follow them.
P6.6.e: They inspect the procedure and sample breaches for notifications.

P6.7.o: People can ask who their information has been shared with.
P6.7.a: Be able to produce, on request, the disclosures made of a person's information.
P6.7.e: They inspect the process and sample requests.

P7.1.o: Decisions based on wrong data can harm people.
P7.1.a: Validate personal information at collection and let people update it.

P8.1.o: People need a way to raise privacy concerns, and the company needs to check it keeps its promises.
P8.1.a: Provide a privacy contact, log and resolve complaints, and review privacy compliance every year.
P8.1.e: They sample complaints and inspect the annual privacy review.

CO1.o: SOC 1 covers controls that matter to your customers' financial statements. Access to the systems that process their transactions is the first thing user auditors look at.
CO1.a: Restrict access to in-scope applications, databases and operating systems; approve new access; remove leavers promptly; review access every quarter; control privileged accounts.
CO1.e: They test new access approvals, timely removals, quarterly reviews and privileged account restrictions across the period.
CO1.r: Access requests; leaver tickets; quarterly access reviews; privileged account lists.

CO2.o: An untested change to a calculation or interface can misstate every customer's figures.
CO2.a: Ticket every change, test it, get approval before release, and keep developers out of production deployments.
CO2.e: They sample changes for testing and approval, and check segregation between development and production.
CO2.r: Change tickets; test evidence; approvals; deployment access lists.

CO3.o: Customers rely on jobs running when they should and failures being caught.
CO3.a: Schedule jobs, monitor them, alert on failures and record how each failure was resolved.
CO3.e: They sample job failures and check they were investigated and resolved.
CO3.r: Job schedules; monitoring alerts; incident tickets.

CO4.o: Lost transaction data cannot be reported on.
CO4.a: Back up in-scope data on schedule, monitor backup jobs, and test restores.
CO4.e: They inspect backup configuration, failure handling and restore tests.
CO4.r: Backup logs; failure tickets; restore test records.

CO5.o: Physical access can bypass logical controls.
CO5.a: Restrict physical access to authorised people, or rely on the hosting provider's SOC report as a subservice organisation.
CO5.e: They inspect physical access lists or the provider's SOC report and your review of it.
CO5.r: Badge access lists; hosting provider SOC report review.

CO6.o: A new system that processes transactions must be proven correct before customers rely on it.
CO6.a: Test and approve new systems and data migrations, including reconciling migrated data.
CO6.e: They inspect implementation testing and sign-off for systems put live in the period.
CO6.r: Project test plans; user acceptance sign-off; migration reconciliations.

CO7.o: Errors in a client's setup carry into every transaction processed for them.
CO7.a: Set up clients from authorised instructions, have a second person check setup, and keep the evidence.
CO7.e: They sample new client setups and changes to standing data for authorisation and review.
CO7.r: Client instructions; setup checklists; second-person review records.

CO8.o: Input is where most processing errors begin.
CO8.a: Accept transactions only from authorised sources, validate them, and reconcile what was received with what was recorded.
CO8.e: They sample transactions and input reconciliations.
CO8.r: Input validation rules; input reconciliations; exception reports.

CO9.o: Calculations, postings and interfaces must give the right answer.
CO9.a: Configure and test calculations, reconcile interfaces, and review exception reports.
CO9.e: They test calculations and inspect reconciliations and exception handling.
CO9.r: Calculation configuration; interface reconciliations; exception reports with follow-up.

CO10.o: Clients put your reports into their financial statements.
CO10.a: Review reports before release, reconcile them to source data, and control distribution.
CO10.e: They sample client reports for review, reconciliation and correct distribution.
CO10.r: Report review sign-offs; reconciliations; distribution lists.

CO11.o: Unreconciled differences hide errors and fraud.
CO11.a: Reconcile key balances on schedule, have them reviewed, and resolve differences.
CO11.e: They sample reconciliations for timeliness, review and resolution.
CO11.r: Reconciliations with preparer and reviewer sign-off.

CO12.o: Where you carve out a subservice organisation, your report relies on its controls working.
CO12.a: Get and review each subservice organisation's SOC report every year, note exceptions and complementary controls, and act on them.
CO12.e: They inspect your reviews of subservice organisation SOC reports.
CO12.r: Subservice organisation SOC reports; review records; bridge letters.
